fatal_errors: The hypothesis does not reconstruct the target temperature-dependent mechanisms: MSAD-controlled solid-solution strengthening, cryogenic inertial dulling, and high-temperature Cottrell-type Portevin–Le Chatelier pinning.

It incorrectly characterizes L11 ordering as a state in which Cr–Cr nearest neighbors dominate; the cited evidence describes L12 ordering as minimizing Cr–Cr nearest neighbors and L11 as Cr segregation on alternating close-packed planes.
The cited evidence does not establish the full causal claim that converting L11 to L12 increases shear-fault-energy fluctuations and thereby raises yield strength.

Electron diffraction and atom-probe tomography can characterize ordering and composition but do not directly measure local shear-fault-energy fluctuations without an additional validated computational or micromechanical inference.
explanation: This is a coherent alternative hypothesis about CrCoNi short-range order and dislocation pinning, with a reasonably controlled same-composition heat-treatment comparison and measurable mechanical and microscopy outcomes. E1 supports strengthening by spatial shear-fault-energy fluctuations, while E2 supports heat-treatment-dependent L11/L12 ordering and changed slip behavior. However, combining those observations into the specific chain L11-to-L12 transition → larger fault-energy fluctuations → higher yield strength goes beyond the cited evidence. The falsification experiment is useful but overly conjunctive: failure of any one proposed signature would be treated as falsification even though some measurements are indirect. Most importantly, it bears little mechanistic or experimental agreement with the target study, which compared equiatomic FCC single crystals over 9–1373 K using CRSS, strain-rate jumps, TEM, and DFT to isolate lattice-distortion strengthening, low-temperature dislocation inertia, and high-temperature dynamic solute pinning.
